disease_label_per_paper: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome secondary to postpartum endometritis caused by Escherichia coli
presentation_summary: 29-year-old puerpera presented one week after urgent cesarean section and five days after discharge.
Symptoms were fever, right upper quadrant pain worse with movement, pelvic pain, and smelly lochiations.
On readmission temperature was 38.3 C, blood pressure 105/60 mmHg, and pulse 93/min.
Exam showed tenderness in the right upper and lower quadrants, slight cervical motion tenderness, and green smelly vaginal discharge.
Transvaginal ultrasound showed increased uterine volume for puerperal period, thickened heterogeneous endometrium with increased Doppler vascularity, and moderate free fluid in the pouch of Douglas.
Labs showed WBC 12 x10^3/mm3, absolute neutrophils 11 x10^3/mm3 (91%), CRP 15 mg/dL, and normal liver tests.
Abdominal ultrasound showed free fluid in perihepatic, perisplenic, and pelvic spaces; contrast CT showed abnormal endometrial enhancement and Glisson capsule enhancement.
Endocervical culture later grew E. coli; she improved with antibiotics and was discharged on hospital day 8.

clinical_course: Blood cultures and vaginal/endocervical swabs were obtained after admission.
Because postpartum endometritis did not explain RUQ pain, abdominal ultrasound and contrast CT were performed.
She received IV clindamycin and gentamicin from hospital day 2.
After 48 hours, symptoms, temperature, leukocyte count, and CRP improved and therapy was switched to ceftriaxone plus doxycycline.
She was discharged on hospital day 8 with resolution of clinical signs, normal labs, and thin regular endometrium on ultrasound.
At 3- and 6-month follow-up she reported no further symptoms.
actual_treatment: doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days

outcome.source_text_value: full resolution of clinical signs and no further symptoms at follow-up

quality_warnings: Endocervical E. coli culture, negative blood cultures, negative STI swabs, and treatment response are non-ranking confirmatory/treatment-context evidence.
Perihepatitis/RUQ findings are retained as presentation evidence but not made part of the disease name.
Normal liver tests and RUQ pain are preserved to support fair competition with hepatobiliary and perihepatitis mimics.
